collection_summary: This instance is a curated, source-defined ground truth listing the 31 chemical elements first scientifically observed between 1869 (year of Mendeleev's periodic table publication) and 1945 (end of World War II) inclusive, as listed in the canonical chronological-discoveries wikitable of the Wikipedia 'Discovery of the chemical elements' master article. The universe rule strictly uses the source's 'Observed Year' column; 10 elements with Observed Year pre-1869 but Isolated Year in 1869-1945 (Fluorine, Titanium, Cerium, Thorium, Lanthanum, Neodymium, Erbium, Terbium, Caesium, Helium) are excluded. For each element the staged row records the Discovery Year (= Observed Year) — a single-cell-per-row factual lookup. The 31-row universe spans Gallium 1875 (the first Mendeleev-predicted element, validating his periodic table) through Curium and Americium 1944 (Manhattan Project transuranium discoveries) plus Promethium 1945 (completing the rare-earth series).
source_coverage_notes:
Roles:
- source_urls[0] (Discovery_of_the_chemical_elements): universe + filter + value (defines the canonical chronological-discoveries wikitable with 106 parsed rows = 104 element-discovery rows + 2 non-element historical-milestone rows for Lavoisier's 1789 list and Mendeleev's 1869 periodic table arrangement; the 31 staged rows are exactly those element-discovery rows with Observed Year in [1869, 1945]; supplies the per-row Element name verbatim and the Discovery Year as the 4-digit year from the Observed Year column — the Isolated Year column is NOT used as a fallback for this instance, per the cycle-1 strict-Observed-Year-only rule).

Single-source Tier B instance. The master Wikipedia article is the canonical compilation of chemical-element discovery dates and discoverers, drawing on the historical chemistry literature (e.g., the Wieser/Coplen IUPAC technical reports, the Royal Society of Chemistry's element profiles). Per-element Wikipedia articles exist (Hydrogen, Gallium, etc.) and would supply additional attributes like discoverer name, place of discovery, isotopes, properties — but the staged 2-col schema needs only Discovery Year and the master article supplies that cleanly via its 'Observed Year' column. Cell-level audit can spot-check by reading the master article's chronological table for any of the 31 elements.
decision_log:
Candidate card (per instance_selection_priorities.md):
- Pre-gate verdict: Pass. Universe (31 chemical elements discovered 1869-1945) is fully source-defined via the cited master article's chronological wikitable and the explicit temporal filter; partition rule (per element) is source-defined; per-row attribute cells are source-defined via the Element column and Observed Year column. Table is LLM-knowable for a pre-2025 cutoff: very-LLM-knowable rows include the canonical Mendeleev-predicted trio (Gallium 1875, Scandium 1879, Germanium 1886), the noble gases (Argon 1894, Neon/Krypton/Xenon 1898), and the radioactive trio (Polonium/Radium 1898); harder calibration cells include the lanthanide rare-earths (Praseodymium 1885, Dysprosium 1886, etc.) and the early transuranium discoveries (Technetium 1937, Francium 1939, Astatine 1940). Row count (31) is comfortably above the 10-row gate and is a different row-count band from the existing factual_lookup instance `eu_member_states_accession_years` (27 rows × 2 cols, Country → Year of EU Accession), which is structurally the closest analog.
- Seed/provenance: original instance, NOT from a seed in example_questions.txt. User selected this from a slate of 6 factual_lookup #2 candidate angles (largest country per continent, Seven Summits, currencies by GDP, African official languages, G20 national symbols, **chemical-elements discovery years 1869-1945**). The user picked variant F (chemical elements 1869-1945) — the most distinctive entity class among the candidates.
- Category: factual_lookup (gap 4 after the 2026-05-12 tier-simplification refresh raised the target from 3 to 5; this instance brings the category from gap 4 to gap 3) primary; temporal (gap 3) secondary because the 1875-1945 discovery-year axis is a meaningful temporal dimension. Per references/artifact-contract.md, factual_lookup pairs canonically with operation_type=projection; the db_analog 'SELECT element, observed_year FROM chemical_elements WHERE observed_year BETWEEN 1869 AND 1945' is the canonical single-attribute-per-row lookup over a temporally-filtered universe.
- Source plan: Tier B Wikipedia, single source URL; gt_construction = manual_wikipedia; source_count = 1.
- Expected shape: 31 rows × 2 columns; PK = Element.
- Domain: Science/Chemistry — new subdomain under the Science family (Science previously had 7 instances across 6 subdomains: Academia ×2, Astronomy, History of Science, Mathematics, Physics, Space Exploration ×2 — Chemistry adds a 7th subdomain). The Chemistry subdomain has no existing instance; this staging plants Chemistry as a new Science subdomain. Science family extends from 8 instances to 9.
- Risks/adaptation: The 2-col schema is intentionally lean — pure factual_lookup category fit (single-attribute-per-row lookup over a fixed entity set). This matches the existing factual_lookup template `eu_member_states_accession_years` (also 2-col, Country → Year). A multi-col variant (adding Atomic Number or Discoverer) would drift toward multi_attribute_projection category-fit, which is now saturated at 8/8 target — staging factual_lookup #2 in the cleanest 2-col shape avoids category-fit ambiguity. The Discovery Year cell is the 'Observed Year' from the source (year of first scientific observation), not the 'Isolated Year' (which can differ — e.g., Gallium was observed and isolated both in 1875, but some elements have Observed/Isolated years that differ by months or years). The choice to prefer Observed Year matches the standard chemistry-history convention.
- Decision: Stage.

Why original rather than seed-driven: no seed in example_questions.txt targets `factual_lookup` directly (the existing factual_lookup instance `eu_member_states_accession_years` was an original concept, and the picker doesn't enumerate factual-lookup seeds because they're the easiest category to assemble from any factual-knowledge axis).

Why this shape (chemistry/1869-1945) rather than alternatives: among 6 candidate angles presented to the user, the chemistry-elements angle was chosen for two main reasons: (a) new entity class (chemical elements) — picker's entity-class diversification axis explicitly flagged 'animals/species, chemical compounds, ...' as underrepresented; (b) clean source structure — the Wikipedia master article has a 106-row chronological wikitable with Element and Observed Year columns that map directly to the staged schema, requiring no curator interpretation. The 1869-1945 window is meaningful as the 'post-Mendeleev pre-WWII era' and yields 31 rows comfortably above the 10-row gate.

Why 2-col rather than 3-col (with Atomic Number) or 4-col (with Discoverer): the existing factual_lookup template is 2-col (eu_member_states_accession_years: Country | Year). Matching that template preserves category-fit clarity (factual_lookup = single-attribute-per-row lookup) and avoids drift toward multi_attribute_projection. The trade-off is that 2-col schemas have low calibration capacity per row, but factual_lookup is the category that explicitly tests single-cell recall, so the thin schema is the appropriate shape.

Why Observed Year rather than Isolated Year: the source's chronological table has both columns. The standard chemistry-history convention uses Observed Year (year of first scientific observation/identification) as the canonical 'discovery year' rather than Isolated Year (year of first pure isolation, which can be later). In the 1869-1945 window, the two years coincide for most elements but differ by months/years for some — the staged Year cell uses Observed Year consistently to match the historical chemistry literature's standard.

Why 1869-1945 window rather than other temporal boundaries: 1869 is the year of Mendeleev's periodic table publication, marking the conceptual boundary of the 'modern chemistry' era where elements were predicted before being discovered. 1945 is the end of WWII, which roughly marks the end of the first synthetic-elements era (the Manhattan Project's transuranium discoveries). The 1875-1945 actual data range starts with Gallium 1875 (the first Mendeleev-predicted element) and ends with Promethium 1945 (completing the rare-earth lanthanide series). Alternative windows considered: 1800-1900 (43 rows, 19th-century-only), 1800-1925 (48 rows, pre-quantum-mechanics), 1869-1925 (24 rows, Mendeleev to Modern); the 1869-1945 window has the cleanest narrative anchor (Mendeleev to WWII end) and yields the right row count for factual_lookup (~30 rows).

Category ↔ operation_type pairing: factual_lookup pairs canonically with operation_type=projection per references/artifact-contract.md. The single-attribute SELECT over the per-element universe is the canonical factual_lookup primitive.

Domain selection: Science/Chemistry — first instance in the Chemistry subdomain. Science family now has 8 → 9 instances spanning Astronomy, Academia ×2, History of Science, Mathematics, Physics, Space Exploration ×2, and Chemistry (new). The Chemistry subdomain is a natural fit for an element-discovery-year instance; alternative classification under History/Science would be defensible but the strong chemistry focus (specific elements, specific physical/chemical properties) makes Science/Chemistry the operative label.

Post-audit (2026-05-12, cycle 1): the cycle-1 audit raised one BLOCKING and one NON-BLOCKING HYGIENE. (a) BLOCKING — title-vs-rule mismatch: the cycle-0 table_title said 'first observed or isolated between 1869 and 1945' but the actual universe rule filtered on Observed Year only. A literal 'observed or isolated' reading would pull in 10 additional elements whose Observed Year is pre-1869 but whose Isolated Year is in 1869-1945 (Fluorine, Titanium, Cerium, Thorium, Lanthanum, Neodymium, Erbium, Terbium, Caesium, Helium — 10 elements that the staged 31-row universe excludes). Resolved by tightening the table_title to 'first scientifically observed between 1869 and 1945, with the year of first observation' and adding a parenthetical clarification that elements with Observed Year before 1869 but Isolated Year in 1869-1945 are explicitly excluded. The alternative — expanding the universe to 41 rows by including the 10 mismatched elements — was rejected because it would introduce per-row Discovery Year ambiguity (Helium's 'Discovery Year' could be either 1868 Observed or 1895 Isolated; the cleaner choice is to use the chemistry-history convention of Observed Year = canonical 'discovery year'). The 31-row universe matches the now-tightened title-rule. (b) HYGIENE — narrative drift on '106 rows' source-table description: the cycle-0 narrative described tables[4] as '106 rows total covering all elements discovered since 1669' but didn't note that 2 of those 106 parsed rows are non-element historical-milestone entries (Lavoisier's 1789 'first modern list of chemical elements' entry and Mendeleev's 1869 'periodic table arrangement' entry, both with NaN Z/Element cells). Resolved by updating temporal_note and _extraction_notes to clarify: '106 parsed rows total of which 104 are element-discovery rows and 2 are non-element historical-milestone rows', with the pipeline's dropna(subset=['Year','Z']) filter explicitly identified as the step that drops these 2. Net cycle-1 changes: 1 BLOCKING title-tightening + db_analog rewording; 0 row count change (universe was already correct under the strict Observed-Year-only rule); 1 HYGIENE narrative-clarification on source-table structure. Useful reference: 'universe rule that the title overpromises' is a common factual_lookup/temporal-filter pitfall — the title-vs-rule alignment check should happen at Stage-1 staging.

Post-audit (2026-05-12, cycle 3 verification re-audit): the cycle-2 audit returned Ready with 1 HYGIENE (stale collection_summary + source_coverage_notes wording — applied AFTER the cycle-2 audit was written). The user requested a cycle-3 verification audit to confirm the post-cycle-2 HYGIENE was fully applied. The cycle-3 audit confirmed Ready BUT found 2 additional residual HYGIENE issues that the cycle-2 audit and my post-cycle-2 fix had missed: (a) normalization_decisions's Discovery Year normalization paragraph still contained an active 'For rows where the source's Observed Year is missing... the Isolated Year column is the fallback' sentence — even though the staged universe doesn't use Isolated Year as fallback under any condition (the cycle-2 fix corrected the source_coverage_notes Roles block but missed this normalization_decisions sentence); (b) the decision_log Category bullet still quoted the cycle-0 db_analog 'SELECT element, discovery_year FROM chemical_elements WHERE discovery_year BETWEEN 1869 AND 1945' even though the actual db_analog field was updated in cycle 1 to use 'observed_year' — a stale narrative quote of a superseded value. Resolved both: (a) normalization_decisions now states 'The Isolated Year column is NOT used for the staged Discovery Year cell under any condition — this is a strict Observed-Year-only rule (no fallback to Isolated Year, no preference for the later of the two years, no curator interpolation)'; (b) decision_log Category bullet's db_analog quote updated to 'SELECT element, observed_year FROM chemical_elements WHERE observed_year BETWEEN 1869 AND 1945' matching the live db_analog field. Net cycle-3 changes: 0 BLOCKING; 0 row count change; 2 HYGIENE narrative cleanups (1 stale 'Isolated Year fallback' sentence + 1 stale db_analog quote). Useful reference: when a BLOCKING repair updates a field value (db_analog, table_title, etc.), the curator should grep for ALL prior text-quotes of that value across decision_log, _extraction_notes, normalization_decisions, source_coverage_notes, collection_summary, and temporal_note — narrative quotes can lag the actual field value by 1-2 cycles if not explicitly searched.
normalization_decisions: Universe definition: the staged universe is exactly the 31 elements in the master Wikipedia article's chronological-discoveries wikitable (tables[4] per pandas.read_html) whose source's 'Observed Year' column has a year in [1869, 1945] inclusive. The universe rule is STRICTLY based on Observed Year — the 'Isolated Year' column is NOT used for inclusion. The 1869 lower bound is the year of Mendeleev's periodic table publication (the conceptual boundary for 'post-Mendeleev modern chemistry'); the 1945 upper bound is the end of World War II (the conceptual boundary for 'early synthetic-elements era'). The actual data range starts at 1875 (Gallium, first Mendeleev-predicted element) and ends at 1945 (Promethium); the 1869-1874 gap is intrinsic to the source (no element discoveries in those 5 years). Source-table structure note: pandas.read_html parses tables[4] as 106 rows, of which 104 are element-discovery rows and 2 are non-element historical-milestone rows (Lavoisier's 1789 'first modern list of chemical elements' entry and Mendeleev's 1869 'periodic table arrangement' entry, both with NaN Z and Element cells); the pipeline filter drops these 2 via dropna(subset=['Year','Z']). Elements with Observed Year before 1869 (e.g., Hydrogen 1766, Oxygen 1774, Phosphorus 1669, Sodium 1807) are excluded. Elements with Observed Year after 1945 (e.g., Berkelium 1949, Californium 1950, Einsteinium 1952) are excluded. Additionally, 10 elements with Observed Year before 1869 but Isolated Year in 1869-1945 are excluded by the strict Observed-Year-only filter (Fluorine Obs 1771 / Iso 1886, Titanium 1791/1875, Cerium 1803/1875, Thorium 1829/1914, Lanthanum 1838/1904, Neodymium 1841/1901, Erbium 1843/1934, Terbium 1843/1937, Caesium 1860/1882, Helium 1868/1895) — these would be included under a less-strict 'observed OR isolated in 1869-1945' rule but are excluded under the actual 'observed in 1869-1945' rule (see cycle-1 audit and decision_log for the title-vs-rule alignment). Element name normalization: each element's name is taken verbatim from the master table's Element column. No abbreviations or symbol substitutions (e.g., 'Praseodymium' not 'Pr', 'Gadolinium' not 'Gd'). Capitalization preserves the source's convention (each element name starts with a capital letter). Discovery Year normalization: 4-digit integer extracted from the master table's 'Observed Year' column via regex '(\d{4})'. The 'Isolated Year' column is NOT used for the staged Discovery Year cell under any condition — this is a strict Observed-Year-only rule (no fallback to Isolated Year, no preference for the later of the two years, no curator interpolation). Where the source's Observed Year cell contains a range or alternative (e.g., '1898 / 1900' for some elements), the earlier year is taken — but no such case applies to any of the 31 staged rows in this window. The Discovery Year cell is the year of first scientific observation, not the year of first pure isolation (which can differ for some elements; the source's two-column structure makes this distinction explicit and the staged value uses the 'Observed Year' column consistently). Alphabetical sort: the CSV is sorted alphabetically by Element name, matching the standard convention for fixed-entity-list instances in this benchmark (Argon, Astatine, Curium, ..., Xenon, Ytterbium). An alternative sort-by-Atomic-Number ordering was considered but rejected because (a) the Z column is not included in the schema, and (b) alphabetical-by-name is the established convention for this benchmark's entity-list instances.
open_questions: 1. Whether to add an Atomic Number column (3-col schema: Element | Atomic Number | Discovery Year) for richer calibration. The current 2-col schema preserves the cleanest factual_lookup category fit but trades off per-row attribute richness. A v2 could add Atomic Number, but this would drift toward multi_attribute_projection category fit. 2. Whether to add a Discoverer(s) column (4-col schema: Element | Atomic Number | Discovery Year | Discoverer(s)) for a richer 'who discovered each element' angle. This would shift the category fit clearly to multi_attribute_projection — but that category is now saturated at 8/8 so this v2 should not be prioritized. 3. Whether the universe window should be widened to 1750-1945 (covering pre-Mendeleev discoveries like Oxygen 1774, Hydrogen 1766, etc.) for ~60 rows, or narrowed to 1869-1925 (pre-WWII period only) for 24 rows. The 1869-1945 window is the curator's pick for narrative cleanliness (Mendeleev to WWII end) and row count fit. 4. Whether to use 'Isolated Year' rather than 'Observed Year' for the Discovery Year cell. The two columns differ for some elements (the source explicitly maintains both as separate columns); the staged choice prefers Observed Year as the more conventional chemistry-history 'discovery year'. 5. Whether to expand the universe to include 1946-present synthetic elements (Berkelium 1949 through Tennessine 2009 / Oganesson 2002) for a 'modern synthetic-elements era' supplementary instance — this would be a separate instance with its own row set, not a widening of this instance's window. 6. Whether to include all 31 staged elements regardless of whether they're 'naturally occurring' (Z ≤ 92) vs 'synthetic' (Z ≥ 93). The current staging includes both — Technetium Z=43 (synthetic), Francium Z=87 (rare natural), Astatine Z=85 (rare natural), Neptunium/Plutonium/Americium/Curium Z=93-96 (synthetic). A v2 could split into 'naturally occurring elements 1869-1945' vs 'synthetic elements 1937-1945' as two separate instances.
